questions.los: Module 5: Pricing and Valuation of Forward Contracts and for an Underlying with Varying Maturities
questions.stem: The spot price of an asset is $70.00. If the annual risk-free rate is 2.50%, the 9-month forward price is closest to:
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because the forward price is the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate over the life of the contract or F_0(T) = S_0 (1+ r)^T where S_0is the current spot price, r is the risk-free rate and T is time. Therefore, the 9-month forward price is not equal to the spot price divided by (1+ r)^T or £70.00 / (1+ 0.025)^0.75 = £68.72. B.Correct because the forward price is the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate over the life of the contract or F_0(T) = S_0 (1+ r)^T where S_0 is the current spot price, r is the risk-free rate and T is time. Therefore, the 9-month forward price is equal to £70.00 (1+ 0.025)^0.75 = £71.31. C.Incorrect because the forward price is the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate over the life of the contract or F_0(T) = S_0 (1+ r)^T where S_0 is the current spot price, r is the risk-free rate and T is time. Therefore, the 9-month forward price is not equal to the spot price multiplied by (1+ r) (omitting time) or £70.00 (1+.025) = £71.75.

questions.los: Module 5: Pricing and Valuation of Forward Contracts and for an Underlying with Varying Maturities
questions.stem: An investor observes that the price of an underlying asset is $20. The investor immediately enters into forward contract to purchase the underlying asset in one year at a price of $10. At contract initiation, the value of the forward contract is closest to:
questions.explanation: A.Correct because when a forward contract is initiated, neither party pays anything to the other. It is a valueless contract, neither an asset nor a liability. Therefore, its value at initiation is zero. B.Incorrect because the value of a forward contract at expiration is the spot price of the underlying minus the forward price agreed to in the contract. Therefore, this answer choice represents the value of the forward contract at expiration, not at initiation, i.e., $20 - $10 = $10. By contrast, the value of the forward at initiation is zero, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer. C.Incorrect because this answer choice incorrectly assumes that the forward value at contract initiation is the sum of spot price at contract initiation plus forward price at contract initiation, i.e., $20 + $10 = $30. By contrast, the value of the forward at initiation is zero, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer.

questions.los: Module 6: Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
questions.stem: Which of the following derivatives realize a gain as the market reference rate rises above the initial fixed rate?
questions.option_b: Short interest rate futures contracts only
questions.option_c: Both long forward rate agreements and short interest rate futures contracts
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because short interest rate futures contracts also gain from a rising market reference rate. B Incorrect because long forward rate agreements also gain from a rising market reference rate. C Correct because realizing a gain on the FRA contract as rates rise. Note that this would be equivalent to taking a short position on a CNY MRR futures contract if one were available. A long FRA (i.e., FRA floating-rate receiver (fixed-rate payer)) position realizes a gain as MRR rises. A short futures contract price is based on (100 − yield), which gains as yield-to-maturity (MRR) rises.

questions.los: Module 6: Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
questions.stem: A futures contract’s:
questions.option_a: mark-to-market is not settled until maturity
questions.option_b: price remains fixed until the contract matures
questions.option_c: variation margin reduces counterparty credit risk
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because forward (not future) contract MTM is not settled until maturity. B Incorrect because the forward price, F 0 (T), is constant until the contract matures, whereas the futures price, f 0 (T), fluctuates daily based upon market changes. C Correct because the daily settlement mechanism resets the futures MTM to zero, and variation margin is exchanged to settle the difference, reducing counterparty credit risk.

questions.los: Module 6: Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
questions.stem: The differential between forward and futures prices is determined by which of the following?
questions.option_b: The correlation between futures prices and interest rates only
questions.option_c: Both interest rate volatility and the correlation between futures prices and interest rates
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because the differential between forward and futures prices is determined by both the correlation between futures prices and interest rates, and by interest rate volatility, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer. B Incorrect because the differential between forward and futures prices is determined by both the correlation between futures prices and interest rates, and by interest rate volatility, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer. C Correct because the different patterns of cash flows for forwards and futures can lead to a difference in the pricing of forwards versus futures. Forward and futures prices are identical under certain conditions, namely: ■ if interest rates are constant, or ■ if futures prices and interest rates are uncorrelated. On the other hand, violations of these assumptions can give rise to differences in pricing between these two contracts. For example, if futures prices are positively correlated with interest rates, long futures contracts are more attractive than long forward positions for the same underlying and maturity. The reason is because rising prices lead to futures profits that are reinvested in periods of rising interest rates, and falling prices lead to losses that occur in periods of falling interest rates. The price differential will also vary with the volatility of interest rates. Therefore, the differential between forward and futures prices is determined by both interest rate volatility and the correlation between futures prices and interest rates.

questions.los: Module 6: Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
questions.stem: An analyst gathers the following information: ■The current spot price of crude oil is $120 per barrel. ■The risk-free rate is 3% with annual compounding. ■A futures contract has 182 days until settlement. ■The storage cost is $5 per barrel, payable at the end of the futures contract. Based on 365 days per year, the futures price per barrel of crude oil is closest to:
questions.explanation: A Correct because the futures price for a commodity with known storage cost amounts may be determined [as …]: f 0 (T) = [S 0 + PV 0 (C)] × (1 + r) T . PV 0 (C) = $5×(1 + 3%) -182/365 . f 0 (T) = [$120 + $5×(1 + 3%) -182/365 ]×(1 + 3%) 182/365 = $126.781768 ≈ $126.78. B Incorrect because it doesn't discount the storage cost from settlement day to today to find its present value since the futures price for a commodity with known storage cost amounts may be determined as: f 0 (T) = [S 0 + PV 0 (C)] × (1 + r) T . If no discounting is applied to the storage cost, it would be incorrectly assumed to be PV 0 (C) = $5. f 0 (T) = [$120 + $5] × (1 + 3%) 182/365 = $126.856008 ≈ $126.86. C Incorrect because it compounds the storage cost from today to settlement instead of discounting to find its present value since the futures price for a commodity with known storage cost amounts may be determined as: f 0 (T) = [S 0 + PV 0 (C)] × (1 + r) T . If compounding is applied to the storage cost, it would be incorrectly assumed to be PV 0 (C) = $5 × (1 + 3%) 182/365 . f 0 (T) = [$120 + $5 × (1 + 3%) 182/365 ] × (1 + 3%) 182/365 = $126.931351 ≈ $126.93.

questions.los: Module 6: Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
questions.stem: Which of the following interest rate derivatives most likely has the largest convexity bias?
questions.option_a: Forward rate agreement on a 1-month market reference rate
questions.option_b: Forward rate agreement on a 3-month market reference rate
questions.option_c: Interest rate futures contract on a 3-month market reference rate
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because the discounting feature of the FRA, which is not present in the futures contract, leads to a convexity bias that is greater for longer discounting periods. Since the length of the discounting period depends on the maturity of the underlying market reference rate, 1-month market reference rate results in a shorter discounting period than the 3-month rate. Therefore, it will suffer from a smaller convexity bias. B Correct because the discounting feature of the FRA, which is not present in the futures contract, leads to a convexity bias that is greater for longer discounting periods. Since the length of the discounting period depends on the maturity of the underlying market reference rate, 3-month market reference rate results in a longer discounting period than the 1-month rate. C Incorrect because convexity bias does not exist in interest rate futures contracts since their prices are not based on discounting. The futures contract has a fixed linear payoff profile for a given basis point change. On the other hand, the discounting feature of the FRA, which is not present in the futures contract, leads to a convexity bias that is greater for longer discounting periods.

questions.los: Module 6: Pricing and Valuation of Futures Contracts
questions.stem: All else being equal, the price of a forward contract is most likely higher than the price of a futures contract if interest rates are:
questions.option_c: positively correlated with futures prices
questions.explanation: A.Correct because a negative correlation between futures prices and interest rates leads to forwards being more desirable than futures to the long position. The reason is that rising prices lead to futures profits that are reinvested in periods of falling interest rates, and falling prices lead to losses that occur in periods of rising interest rates. It is far better to receive all cash flows at expiration under such conditions than to receive them in the interim periods. This condition makes forwards more attractive than futures. The more desirable contract will tend to have the higher price. Therefore, the price of the forward contract is higher than the price of the futures contract on the same underlying when interest rates are negatively correlated with futures prices. B.Incorrect because if futures prices and interest rates are uncorrelated, forwards and futures prices will be the same. Therefore, the price of the forward contract is not higher than the price of the futures contract if interest rates are uncorrelated with futures prices. C.Incorrect because if futures prices are positively correlated with interest rates, futures contracts are more desirable to holders of long positions than are forwards. The more desirable contract will tend to have the higher price. Therefore, the price of the futures contract is higher than the price of the forward contract, and not the other way around, if interest rates are positively correlated with futures prices.

questions.los: Module 7: Pricing and Valuation of Interest Rates and Other Swaps
questions.stem: A series of forward rate agreements and an interest rate swap contract covering the same periods and using the same market reference rate will most likely have the same:
questions.option_c: settlement cash flows
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because different FRA fixed rates usually exist for different times to maturity. In contrast, a standard interest rate swap has a constant fixed rate over its life, which includes multiple periods. B Correct because similarities between interest rate forwards and swaps include the symmetric payoff profile and the fact that no cash flow is exchanged upfront. C Incorrect because different FRA fixed rates usually exist for different times to maturity. In contrast, a standard interest rate swap has a constant fixed rate over its life, which includes multiple periods and the FRA has a single settlement, which occurs at the beginning of an interest period, while a standard swap has periodic settlements, which occur at the end of each respective period.

questions.los: Module 7: Pricing and Valuation of Interest Rates and Other Swaps
questions.stem: From the fixed-rate receiver's perspective, if the market reference rate increases, the value of a swap contract:
questions.option_c: increases
questions.explanation: A Correct because the fixed-rate receiver pays the market reference rate and receives the par swap par rate. If the market reference rate increases, they are paying more and the value of the contract decreases to them. Another interpretation of an interest rate swap is that the fixed-rate payer (floating-rate receiver) is long a floating-rate note (FRN) priced at the MRR and short a fixed-rate bond with a coupon equal to the fixed swap rate. Similarly, the fixed-rate receiver (floating-rate payer) is long a fixed-rate bond with a coupon equal to the swap rate and short a floating-rate note priced at the MRR. A rise in the expected forward rates after inception will increase the present value of floating payments, while the fixed-swap rate will remain the same. B Incorrect because the fixed-rate receiver pays the market reference rate and receives the swap par rate. If the market reference rate increases, they are paying more and the value of the contract decreases to them, not stays the same. Another interpretation of an interest rate swap is that the fixed-rate payer (floating-rate receiver) is long a floating-rate note (FRN) priced at the MRR and short a fixed-rate bond with a coupon equal to the fixed swap rate. Similarly, the fixed-rate receiver (floating rate payer) is long a fixed-rate bond with a coupon equal to the swap rate and short a floating-rate note priced at the MRR. A rise in the expected forward rates after inception will increase the present value of floating payments, while the fixed-swap rate will remain the same. C Incorrect because the fixed-rate receiver pays the market reference rate and receives the swap par rate. If the market reference rate increases, they are paying more and the value of the contract decreases, not increases, to them. Another interpretation of an interest rate swap is that the fixed-rate payer (floating-rate receiver) is long a floating-rate note (FRN) priced at the MRR and short a fixed-rate bond with a coupon equal to the fixed swap rate. Similarly, the fixed-rate receiver (floating rate payer) is long a fixed-rate bond with a coupon equal to the swap rate and short a floating-rate note priced at the MRR. A rise in the expected forward rates after inception will increase the present value of floating payments, while the fixed-swap rate will remain the same.

questions.los: Module 7: Pricing and Valuation of Interest Rates and Other Swaps
questions.stem: A $10 million interest rate swap with annual payments has a fixed swap rate of 1.95%. The implied forward rates are: Year Implied Forward Rate (%) 1 0.50 2 1.15 3 1.35 The periodic settlement value in Year 3 for the fixed-rate payer is expected to be closest to:
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because an average of the first 3 yearly settlement values is used: = (MRR – s N ) × Notional amount × Period ≠ ([0.0050 + 0.0115 + 0.0135]/3 – 0.0195) × $10,000,000 × 1 = (0.0100 – 0.0195) × $10,000,000 × 1 = –$95,000. B Correct because the periodic settlement value = (MRR – s N ) × Notional amount × Period. The market reference rate (MMR) for Year 3 is 1.35%, thus: = (0.0135 – 0.0195) × $10,000,000 × 1 = –$60,000. C Incorrect because this is the periodic settlement value for the floating-rate payer, not the fixed-rate payer: ≠ (s N – MRR) × Notional amount × Period = (0.0195 – 0.0135) × $10,000,000 × 1 = $60,000.

questions.los: Module 7: Pricing and Valuation of Interest Rates and Other Swaps
questions.stem: A swap is most likely similar to a series of forward contracts when:
questions.option_a: all forward contracts are created with the combined value equal to zero.
questions.option_b: all forward contracts are entered into at the price created in the forward market.
questions.option_c: the value of the long forward contracts are matched with the value of the short forward contracts at each swap payment date.
questions.explanation: A.Correct because, in a swap, each forward contract will be created at the fixed price that corresponds to the fixed price of a swap of the same maturity with payments made at the same dates as the series of forward contracts. That means that some of the forward contracts would have positive values and some would have negative values, but their combined values would equal zero. B.Incorrect because, in a swap, each implicit forward contract is said to be off-market, because it is created at the swap price, not the appropriate forward price, which would be the price created in the forward market. Therefore, the forward contracts are created at the swap price, not at the price created in the forward market. C.Incorrect because, in a swap, each forward contract will be created at the fixed price that corresponds to the fixed price of a swap of the same maturity with payments made at the same dates as the series of forward contracts. That means that some of the forward contracts would have positive values and some would have negative values, but their combined values would equal zero. Therefore, a swap contract is similar to a series of long forward contracts of which some have positive values and some have negative values, but the long forward contracts are not matched with the short forward contracts at each swap payment date.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: The upper bound of a call value is the:
questions.option_b: underlying’s price plus the present value of its exercise price or zero, whichever is greater
questions.option_c: underlying’s price minus the present value of its exercise price or zero, whichever is greater
questions.explanation: A Correct because the upper no-arbitrage bound of a call price is the underlying's spot price. B Incorrect because the lower [not upper] bound of a call price is the underlying’s price minus [not plus] the present value of its exercise price or zero, whichever is greater. Instead, the upper no-arbitrage bound of a call price is the underlying's spot price. C Incorrect because the lower [not upper] bound of a call price is the underlying’s price minus the present value of its exercise price or zero, whichever is greater. Instead, the upper no-arbitrage bound of a call price is the underlying's spot price.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: A put option with the greatest moneyness has a strike price:
questions.option_a: less than the price of the underlying
questions.option_b: equal to the price of the underlying
questions.option_c: greater than the price of the underlying
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because when the underlying has not reached the exercise price (currently lower for a call, higher for a put), the option is said to be out-of-the-money. Only in-the-money puts have moneyness. B.Incorrect because when the underlying is precisely at the exercise price, the option is said to be at-the-money. Only in-the-money put options have moneyness. C.Correct because hen the underlying is beyond the exercise price in the appropriate direction (higher for a call, lower for a put), the option is said to be in-the-money. In addition, for puts to expire in-the-money, the value of the underlying must fall below the exercise price. The higher the exercise price, the better chance the underlying has of getting below it. Likewise, if the value of the underlying does fall below the exercise price, the higher the exercise price, the greater the payoff. So, if X is higher,S_T will be below it more often, and if S_T is less than X, the payoff of X – S_T is greater, the higher is X for whatever value of S_T occurs. Therefore, a put option with the greatest moneyness has a strike price greater than the price of the underlying.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: All else being equal, if the risk-free rate increases, the value of a European put option:
questions.option_c: increases
questions.explanation: A.Correct because the value of a European put is inversely related to the risk-free interest rate. Therefore, an increase in the risk-free rate decreases the value of a European put option. B.Incorrect because the value of a European put option does not remain the same if the risk-free rate increases; its value decreases, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer. C.Incorrect because the value of a European put option does not increase if the risk-free rate increases; its value decreases, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: The value of a long position in a European put option is directly related to the:
questions.option_c: value of the underlying
questions.explanation: A.Correct because the value of a European put option is directly related to the exercise price. B.Incorrect because the value of a European put is inversely related to the risk-free interest rate, not directly related. C.Incorrect because the value of a European put option is inversely related to the value of the underlying, not directly related.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: The upper bound of a put value is the:
questions.option_c: present value of the exercise price minus the spot price
questions.explanation: A.Correct because the exercise price, X, therefore represents the upper bound on the put value. B.Incorrect because this is the upper bound of a call price, not a put value. The call buyer will not pay more for the right to purchase an underlying than the price of that underlying, which is the upper bound. C.Incorrect because this distractor represents the lower bound of a put value and not the upper bound, as the lower bound is the present value of the exercise price minus the spot price or zero, whichever is greater.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: The value of a European call option is inversely related to the:
questions.option_c: risk-free interest rate
questions.explanation: A.Correct because the value of a European call option is inversely related to the exercise price. B.Incorrect because the value of a European call option is directly related to the time to expiration. Therefore, a European call option is not inversely related to the time to expiration. C.Incorrect because the value of a European call is directly related to the risk-free interest rate. Therefore, a European call option is not inversely related to the risk-free interest rate.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: All, else held equal, the value of a European call option is best characterized as having a:
questions.option_a: negative relationship with the price of the underlying
questions.option_b: negative relationship with the volatility of the underlying
questions.option_c: positive relationship with the time to expiration
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect. The value of a European call option is directly related to the price of the underlying. B.Incorrect. The value of a European call option is directly related to the volatility of the underlying. C.Correct. The value of a European call option is directly related to the time to expiration. That is, all else held equal, the value of a European call option is higher the longer the time to expiration.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: If the price of the underlying is $57, which of the following long option positions is out of the money? A:
questions.option_a: put with a strike price of $60
questions.option_b: put with a strike price of $50
questions.option_c: call with a strike price of $50
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because when the underlying is beyond the exercise price in the appropriate direction (higher for a call, lower for a put), the option is said to be in-the-money. As the underlying price of $57 is lower than the strike price of $60, the put is in the money, not out of the money. B.Correct because when the underlying has not reached the exercise price (currently lower for a call, higher for a put), the option is said to be out-of-the-money. In this case, as the underlying price of $57 is higher than the strike price of $50, the put is out of the money. C.Incorrect because when the underlying is beyond the exercise price in the appropriate direction (higher for a call, lower for a put), the option is said to be in-the-money. In this case, as the underlying price of $57 is higher than the strike price of $50, the call is in the money, not out of the money.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: Which of the following European options has the greatest value at expiration? A:
questions.option_a: call with an exercise price of 72 and an underlying priced at 83
questions.option_b: call with an exercise price of 83 and an underlying priced at 70
questions.option_c: put with an exercise price of 70 and an underlying priced at 83
questions.explanation: A.Correct because the value of the call option at expiration is the greater of either zero or the underlying price at expiration minus the exercise price, which is typically written as: C_T = Max(0,S_T – X), where C_T= call option price at expiration and S_T= underlying price at expiration. Therefore, a call option with an exercise price of 72 and an underlying priced at 83 will have a value: C_T = Max(0, 83 – 72)= 11. B.Incorrect because, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer, the value of the call option at expiration is: C_T = Max(0,S_T – X). Therefore, a call option with an exercise price of 83 and an underlying priced at 70 will have a value: C_T = Max(0, 70 – 83)= 0, which is less than 11 for the case of the correct answer. C.Incorrect because the put is worth the greater of either zero or the exercise price minus the price of the underlying at expiration. That is, P_T = Max(0,X – S_T). Therefore, a European put with an exercise price of 70 and an underlying priced at 83 will have a value: P_T = Max (0,70 – 83)= 0, which is less than 11 for the case of the correct answer.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: All else being equal, if the exercise values of a European call option and a European put option on the same underlying are equal, both options must be:
questions.option_c: out-of-the-money options
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because the exercise value of a European call is the greater of zero or the value of the underlying minus the exercise price. And the exercise value of a European put is the greater of zero or the exercise price minus the value of the underlying. This means if the call option is in-the-money (out-of-money), the put option on the same strike will be out-of-the money (in-the-money). That is, if the exercise value of a call (put) option is positive, the exercise value of a put (call) option will be zero. Therefore, all else being equal, if the exercise values of a European call option and a European put option are the same, then the European call and the European put cannot both be in-the-money options. B.Correct because the value of a European call at expiration is the exercise value, which is the greater of zero or the value of the underlying minus the exercise price. And the value of a European put at expiration is the exercise value, which is the greater of zero or the exercise price minus the value of the underlying. This means if the call option is in-the-money (out-of-the-money), the put option of the same strike will be out-of-the money (in-the-money). That is, if the exercise value of a call (put) option is positive, the exercise value of a put (call) option will be zero. But when the underlying is precisely at the exercise price (the option is said to be at-the-money), the exercise value of a European call and a European put will the same, which is zero. Therefore, all else being equal, if the exercise values of a European call option and a European put option are the same, then the European call and the European put must be both at-the-money options. C.Incorrect because the exercise value of a European call is the greater of zero or the value of the underlying minus the exercise price. And the exercise value of a European put is the greater of zero or the exercise price minus the value of the underlying. This means if the call option is in-the-money (out-of-money), the put option on the same strike will be out-of-the money (in-the-money). That is, if the exercise value of a call (put) option is positive, the exercise value of a put (call) option will be zero. Therefore, all else being equal, if the exercise values of a European call option and a European put option are the same, then the European call and the European put cannot both be out-of-the money options.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: The current price of the underlying is $7.40 and the annual risk-free rate is 6%. The minimum price for a 6-month call option with a strike price of $7.50 is closest to:
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because the price for a European call option is known to satisfy the formula C_0 ≥ Max[0, S_0– X/(1 + r)^T] where C_0 is the current price of the European call option, S_0 is the current stock price, X is the strike price, r is the risk-free interest rate and T is time. The minimum price is therefore not equal to Max [0,S_0 – X] = Max[0,$7.40 – $7.50] = Max[0,−$0.10] = $0.00. B Correct because the price for a European call option is known to satisfy the formula C_0 ≥ Max[0, S_0– X/(1 + r)^T] where C_0 is the current price of the European call option, S_0 is the current stock price, X is the strike price, r is the risk-free interest rate and T is time. Therefore the minimum price is equal to Max[0,$7.40 – $7.50/(1.06)^6/12] = Max[0,$7.40 – $7.28] = Max[0,$0.12] = $0.12. C Incorrect because the price for a European call option is known to satisfy the formula C_0 ≥ Max[0, S_0– X/(1 + r)^T] where C_0 is the current price of the European call option, S_0 is the current stock price, X is the strike price, r is the risk-free interest rate and T is time. The minimum price therefore is not equal to Max[0, S_0– X/(1 + r)^T] = Max[0,$7.50 – ($7.40/(1.06)^6/12)] = Max[0,$7.50 – $7.19] = $0.31.

questions.los: Module 8: Pricing and Valuation of Options
questions.stem: For a European call option with one month until expiration, if the spot price is below the exercise price, the call option most likely has:
questions.option_c: both positive time value and positive intrinsic value
questions.explanation: A.Correct because a European call option with two months until expiration will typically have positive time value, where time value reflects the value of the uncertainty that arises from the volatility in the underlying. In addition, C_T = Max (0, S_T – X) or intrinsic value equals the greater of zero or the value of the underlying minus exercise price. The call option is out-of-the-money and therefore, has zero intrinsic value. B.Incorrect because the option has zero intrinsic value, as explained in the correct answer. C.Incorrect because the option has zero intrinsic value, as explained in the correct answer.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: An analyst gathers the following information: Call price $10 Stock price $40 Exercise price $60 Interest rate 3% Time to expiry 1 year According to put-call parity, the price of the put is closest to:
questions.explanation: A Correct because S 0 + p 0 = c 0 + X / (1+r) T . This relationship is known as put-call parity. Here S 0 is the spot price, p 0 is the put premium, X is the strike price and r is the interest rate. S 0 + p 0 = c 0 + X / (1+r) T 40 + p 0 = 10 + 60 / 1.03 p 0 = 10 + 60 / 1.03 - 40 = 28.25242718 = 28.25 B Incorrect because S 0 + p 0 = c 0 + X / (1+r) T . This relationship is known as put-call parity. In this response, X was not divided by (1+r) T . Here S 0 is the spot price, p 0 is the put premium, X is the strike price and r is the interest rate. S 0 + p 0 = c 0 + X / (1+r) T 40 + p 0 = 10 + 60 p 0 = 10 + 60 - 40 = 30.00 C Incorrect because S 0 + p 0 = c 0 + X / (1+r) T . This relationship is known as put-call parity. In this response, S 0 was incorrectly added instead of subtracted from c 0 + X / (1+r) T to arrive at P 0 . Here S 0 is the spot price, p 0 is the put premium, X is the strike price and r is the interest rate. S 0 + p 0 = c 0 + X / (1+r) T 40 + p 0 = 10 + 60 / 1.03 p 0 = 10 + 60 / 1.03 + 40 = 108.252427 = 108.25.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: All else being equal, the cost of a fiduciary call must be:
questions.option_a: less than the cost of a synthetic protective put
questions.option_b: equal to the cost of a synthetic protective put
questions.option_c: greater than the cost of a synthetic protective put
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because the cost of the fiduciary call must equal the cost of the synthetic protective put, giving us what is referred to as put–call–forward parity. B.Correct because the cost of the fiduciary call must equal the cost of the synthetic protective put, giving us what is referred to as put–call–forward parity. C.Incorrect because the cost of the fiduciary call must equal the cost of the synthetic protective put, giving us what is referred to as put–call–forward parity.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: All else being equal, based on put-call–forward parity, the price of a put is higher than the price of a call when:
questions.option_a: the forward price of the underlying is lower than the exercise price
questions.option_b: the forward price of the underlying is equal to the exercise price
questions.option_c: the forward price of the underlying is higher than the exercise price
questions.explanation: A.Correct because it follows that the cost of the fiduciary call must equal the cost of the synthetic protective put, giving us what is referred to as put–call–forward parity, F_0(T)/(1 + r)^T + P_0 = C_0 + X/(1 + r)^T. Rearranging this equation results in: P_0 - C_0 = [X – F_0(T)]/(1 + r)^T. Based on this parity equation, P_0 > C_0 when X > F_0(T). B.Incorrect because, according to put–call–forward parity, the price of a put is higher than the price of a call when when the forward price is lower, not equal to, than the exercise price. The put–call–forward parity is presented as: P_0 - C_0 = [X – F_0(T)]/(1 + r)^T. C.Incorrect because, according to put–call–forward parity, the price of a put is higher than the price of a call when the forward price is lower, not higher, than the exercise price. questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: According to put–call parity, a long put option is equivalent to being:
questions.option_a: long a call, short the underlying asset, and long a risk-free bond
questions.option_b: long a call, long the underlying asset, and short a risk-free bond
questions.option_c: short a call, long the underlying asset, and long a risk-free bond
questions.explanation: A.Correct because the formula for put–call parity is S_0 + P_0= C_0 + X/(1 + r)^T, where S_0 is the stock price at time zero, P_0 is the price of a put option at time zero, C_0 is the price of a call option at time zero, X is the strike price, r is the risk-free rate, and T is time. By using the symbols and the signs in these versions of put–call parity, we can see several important interpretations. In the equations below, plus signs mean long and minus signs mean short: P_0 = C_0 − S_0 + X/(1 + r)^T ⇒ long put = long call, short asset, long bond. B.Incorrect because a long put option is not equivalent to being long a call, long the underlying asset, and short a risk-free bond. By using the symbols and the signs in these versions of put–call parity, we can see several important interpretations. In the equations below, plus signs mean long and minus signs mean short: P_0 = C_0 − S_0 + X/(1 + r)^T⇒ long put = long call, short asset, long bond. C.Incorrect because a long put option is not equivalent to being short a call, long the underlying asset, and long a risk-free bond. By using the symbols and the signs in these versions of put–call parity, we can see several important interpretations. In the equations below, plus signs mean long and minus signs mean short: P_0 = C_0 − S_0 + X/(1 + r)^T⇒ long put = long call, short asset, long bond.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: Which of the following is most accurate? Put-call-forward parity:
questions.option_a: assumes that the strike of the options is equal to the forward price of the underlying
questions.option_b: is derived by equating the price of an at the money put to the price of an at the money call
questions.option_c: assumes that the maturity of the put option, the call option, the forward and the bond are the same
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because the put-call-forward parity equation is valid for all strikes. P_0 - C_0 = [X - F_0(T)]/(1 + r)^T, X is the strike and can take any value. B.Incorrect because the put-call-forward parity equation is formed by comparing the maturity payoffs of synthetic protective put and a fiduciary call. Because we showed that the fiduciary call is equivalent to the protective put, a fiduciary call has to be equivalent to a protective put with a forward contract. It follows that the cost of the fiduciary call must equal the cost of the synthetic protective put, giving us what is referred to as put–call–forward parity. C.Correct because the put-call-forward parity equation is formed by comparing the maturity payoffs of synthetic protective put and a fiduciary call. It follows that maturity of all the components have to be the same. Because we showed that the fiduciary call is equivalent to the protective put, a fiduciary call has to be equivalent to a protective put with a forward contract. It follows that the cost of the fiduciary call must equal the cost of the synthetic protective put, giving us what is referred to as put–call–forward parity.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity

This implies that a short underlying position is equivalent to: −S_0 = -C_0 + P_0 -X/(1 + r)^T, that is, a short call, a long put, and a short (not long) bond. B.Correct because the put-call parity relationship implies that a long underlying can be mimicked as follows: S_0 = C_0 – P_0 + X/(1 + r)^T. This implies that a short underlying position is equivalent to: −S_0 = -C_0 + P_0 -X/(1 + r)^T, that is, a short call, a long put, and a short bond. C.Incorrect because the put-call parity relationship implies that a long underlying can be mimicked as follows: S_0 = C_0 – P_0 + X/(1 + r)^T. This implies that a short underlying position is equivalent to: −S_0 = -C_0 + P_0 -X/(1 + r)^T, that is, a short (not long) call, a long (not short) put, and a short bond.

Rearranging the formula yields: -X(1 + r)^−T = C_0- P_0 - F_0(T)(1 + r)^−T In other words, one can create a synthetic short position in a risk–free bond by going long a call, short a put, and short a forward contract. In other words, under put–call parity, at t = 0 the price of the long underlying asset plus the long put must equal the price of the long call plus the risk-free asset. Rearranging the formula yields: -X(1 + r)^−T = C_0- P_0 - F_0(T)(1 + r)^−T In other words, one can create a synthetic short position in a risk–free bond by going long a call, short a put, and short a forward contract.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: According to put-call parity, the payoff of a long risk-free bond can be replicated synthetically by going:
questions.option_a: long an asset, long a put and long a call
questions.option_b: long an asset, long a put and short a call

Therefore, the payoff of a long risk-free bond cannot be synthetically created by going long an asset, long a put and long a call. B.Correct because according to put-call parity, X/(1 + r)^T = S_0 + P_0 – C_0, long bond = long asset, long put, short call. Therefore, the payoff of a long risk-free bond can be synthetically created by going long an asset, long a put and short a call. C.Incorrect because according to put-call parity, X/(1 + r)^T = S_0 + P_0 – C_0, long bond = long asset, long put, short call. Therefore, the payoff of a long risk-free bond cannot be synthetically created by going long an asset, short a put and short a call.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: A fiduciary call is a strategy in which a trader purchases a call option:
questions.option_a: and takes a short position in the underlying asset
questions.option_b: with funds received from selling short a zero coupon bond of the same maturity as the call option
questions.option_c: along with a zero coupon bond of the same maturity as the call option and with a face value equal to the exercise price of the option
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because in a fiduciary call the investor, buys a call option on this asset with an exercise price of X that expires at T and a risk-free zero-coupon bond with a face value of X that matures at T. This strategy is sometimes known as a fiduciary call. B.Incorrect because in a fiduciary call the investor, buys a call option on this asset with an exercise price of X that expires at T and a risk-free zero-coupon bond with a face value of X that matures at T. This strategy is sometimes known as a fiduciary call. C.Correct because this combination of instruments is the precise definition of a fiduciary call. At time 0, this investor buys a call option on this asset with an exercise price of X that expires at T and a risk-free zero-coupon bond with a face value of X that matures at T. This strategy is sometimes known as a fiduciary call.

questions.los: Module 9: Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity
questions.stem: According to put-call-forward parity, the payoff on a synthetic protective put is equivalent to the payoff on a portfolio consisting of:
questions.option_a: a long call and a long risk-free bond.
questions.option_b: a long call, a short forward contract and a long risk-free bond.
questions.option_c: a long put, a short forward contract and a short risk-free bond.
questions.explanation: A.Correct because recall our put–call parity discussion and assume that Investor A creates his protective put in a slightly different manner. Instead of buying the asset, he buys a forward contract and a risk-free bond in which the face value is the forward price. This strategy is a synthetic protective put. Because we showed that the fiduciary call is equivalent to the protective put, a fiduciary call has to be equivalent to a protective put with a forward contract. Therefore, the payoff on a synthetic protective put = the payoff on a fiduciary call, synthetic protective put = long risk-free bond + long forward contract + long put = long call + long risk-free bond. B.Incorrect because recall our put–call parity discussion and assume that Investor A creates his protective put in a slightly different manner. Instead of buying the asset, he buys a forward contract and a risk-free bond in which the face value is the forward price. This strategy is a synthetic protective put. Because we showed that the fiduciary call is equivalent to the protective put, a fiduciary call has to be equivalent to a protective put with a forward contract. Therefore, the payoff on a synthetic protective put is not equal to the payoff on a portfolio consisting of a long call, a short forward contract and a long risk-free bond. C.Incorrect because recall our put–call parity discussion and assume that Investor A creates his protective put in a slightly different manner. Instead of buying the asset, he buys a forward contract and a risk-free bond in which the face value is the forward price. This strategy is a synthetic protective put. Because we showed that the fiduciary call is equivalent to the protective put, a fiduciary call has to be equivalent to a protective put with a forward contract. Therefore, the payoff on a synthetic protective put is not equal to the payoff on a portfolio consisting of a long put, a short forward contract and a short risk-free bond.

questions.los: Module 10: Valuing a Derivative Using a One-Period Binomial Model
questions.stem: An analyst collects the following information: Current stock price €26 Gross return from an up move 1.10 Gross return from a down move 0.75 Call and put exercise price €22 Based on a one-period binomial pricing model, which of the following has the largest payoff?
questions.option_a: Put option following an up move
questions.option_b: Put option following a down move
questions.option_c: Call option following a down move
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because the payoff of a put option following an up move is p 1 u = Max (0, X – S 1 u ) where X is the exercise price and S 1 u is the price after an up move. In this case, S 1 u = €26(1.10) = €28.60. So, p 1 u = Max(0, €22 - €28.60) = €0, which is less than the payoff of a put option following a down move, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer. B Correct because the payoff of a put option following a down move is p 1 d = Max (0, X – S 1 d ) where X is the exercise price and S 1 d is the price after a down move. In this case, S 1 d = €26(0.75) = €19.50. So, p 1 d = Max (0, €22 - €19.50) = €2.50, which is greater than the payoffs of other two responses. C Incorrect because the payoff of a call option following an a down move is c 1 d = Max (0, S 1 d - X) where X is the exercise price and S 1 d is the price after a down move. In this case, S 1 d = €26(0.75) = €19.50. So, c 1 d = Max (0,€19.50 - €22) = €0, which is less than the payoff of a put option following a down move, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer.

questions.los: Module 10: Valuing a Derivative Using a One-Period Binomial Model
questions.stem: An analyst gathers the following information about an underlying: Current price of underlying asset $16.0 End of period upward price $22.0 End of period downward price $12.0 Risk-free rate 4.0% Using a one-period binomial model, the risk-neutral probability of a price increase is closest to:
questions.explanation: A Incorrect because this is the expected return of an upward price move, i.e. S 1 u / S 0 – 1 = $22/$16 – 1 = 1.375 – 1 = 0.375 ≈ 0.38. Instead, the risk neutral probability is equal to 0.46, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer. B Correct because the risk-neutral probability (π) is the computed probability used in binomial option pricing by which the discounted weighted sum of expected values of the underlying, S 1 u = R u S 0 and S 1 d = R d S 0 , equal the current option price. Specifically, this probability is computed using the risk-free rate and assumed up gross return and down gross return of the underlying as in Equation 7. π = 1 + r – R d / R u – R d More specifically, π, is the risk-neutral probability of an increase in the underlying price to S 1 u = R u S 0 , and (1 − π) is that of a decrease, S 1 d = R d S 0 . Thus, An increase from $16 to $22 or a decrease from $16 to $12 corresponds to: R u = $22/$16 = 1.375 and R d = $12/$16 = 0.75. Using the risk-neutral probability (π) of a price increase: π = 1 + r – R d / R u – R d = (1 + 0.04 – 0.75) / (1.375 – 0.75) = 0.29/0.625 = 0.464 ≈ 0.46. C Incorrect because this is the risk-neutral probability of a price decrease (1 − π) = 1 − 0.46 = 0.54. Instead, the risk neutral probability is equal to 0.46, as described in the response rationale for the correct answer.

Specifically, this probability is computed using the risk-free rate and assumed up gross return and down gross return of the underlying as in π= (1+r-R d )/(R u -R d ). questions.stem: Venture capital is best classified as a sub-category of:
questions.option_c: private equity.

B.Incorrect because hedge funds are private investment vehicles that manage portfolios of securities and/or derivative positions using a variety of strategies. questions.option_b: fall outside of the definition of long-only positions in stocks, bonds, and cash.
questions.option_c: have relatively high correlation of returns with those of traditional investments.
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because alternative assets, by their very nature, tend to be less efficiently priced than traditional marketable securities, providing an opportunity to exploit market inefficiencies through active management. B.Correct because investing in alternative assets can require handling illiquidity, transacting on private markets, operating sophisticated investment strategies, or risk–return profiles that are very different from those of traditional long-only investments. C.Incorrect because alternative investments often have Relatively low correlation of returns with those of traditional investments.

questions.stem: Management fees are most likely based on assets under management for:
questions.option_c: both hedge funds and private equity funds.
questions.explanation: A.Correct because funds are generally structured with a management fee typically ranging from 1% to 2% of assets under management (e.g. for hedge funds) or committed capital (e.g. private equity funds), which is how much money in total that LP's have committed to the fund's future investments. B.Incorrect because funds are generally structured with a management fee typically ranging from 1% to 2% of assets under management (e.g. for hedge funds) or committed capital (e.g. private equity funds), which is how much money in total that LP's have committed to the fund's future investments. C.Incorrect because funds are generally structured with a management fee typically ranging from 1% to 2% of assets under management (e.g. for hedge funds) or committed capital (e.g. private equity funds), which is how much money in total that LP's have committed to the fund's future investments.

questions.los: Module 1: Alternative Investment Features, Methods, and Structures
questions.stem: A feature that protects hedge fund clients from paying twice for the same performance is most likely a:
questions.option_c: high-water mark.
questions.explanation: A. Incorrect because hedge fund managers may discount their fees for larger investors or for placement agents who introduced these investors. However, a rebate does not, in isolation, protect clients from paying twice for the same performance. B.Incorrect because the partnership agreement usually specifies that the performance fee is earned only after the fund achieves a return known as a hurdle rate. The hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return, typically 8%, that the GP must exceed in order to earn the performance fee. GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded. C.Correct because in hedge funds, fee calculations also take into account a high-water mark, which reﬂects the highest value used to calculate an incentive fee. A high-water mark is the highest value of the fund investment ever achieved at a performance fee crystallization date, net of fees, by the individual LP. A high-water mark clause states that a hedge fund manager must recuperate declines in value from the high-water mark before performance fees can be charged on newly generated profits. The use of high-water marks protects clients from paying twice for the same performance.

questions.los: Module 1: Alternative Investment Features, Methods, and Structures
questions.stem: In co-investing, the investor invests in alternative assets indirectly through a fund but also has the:
questions.option_a: right to invest directly in the same assets alongside the fund.
questions.option_b: obligation to invest directly in the same assets alongside the fund.
questions.option_c: right to invest in the general partner's fund management company.
questions.explanation: A.Correct because in co-investing, the investor invests in assets indirectly through the fund but also possesses rights (known as co-investment rights) to invest directly in the same assets. Through co-investing, an investor is able to make an investment alongside a fund when the fund identifies deals; the investor is not limited to participating in the deal solely by investing in the fund. B.Incorrect because in co-investing, the investor invests in assets indirectly through the fund but also possesses rights (known as co-investment rights) to invest directly in the same assets. However, there is no obligation to invest. C.Incorrect because in co-investing, the investor invests in assets indirectly through the fund but also possesses rights (known as co-investment rights) to invest directly in the same assets, not in the general partner's fund management company.

In co-investing, investors co-invest an additional amount into that same investment often without paying management fees on the capital they used for the direct investment (a co-investment, in this case). B.Incorrect because one of the advantages of co-investing is that it has reduced management fees compared with the fund investing method. C.Incorrect because one of the advantages of co-investing is that it has reduced management fees compared with the fund investing method.

questions.los: Module 1: Alternative Investment Features, Methods, and Structures
questions.stem: A hedge fund feature that allows an incentive fee to be earned only after the fund exceeds a specified return best defines a:
questions.option_c: high-water mark.
questions.explanation: A. Incorrect because investors in modern hedge funds are subject to extended holding periods (known as lockup periods) and subsequent notice periods before an investment redemption is possible. As noted previously, restrictions on redemptions are typically imposed. Investors may be required to keep their money in the hedge fund for a minimum period (referred to as a lockup period) before they are allowed to make withdrawals or redeem shares. B. Correct because the hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return, typically 8%, that the GP must exceed in order to earn the performance fee. GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded. C. Incorrect because in hedge funds, fee calculations also take into account a high-water mark, which reflects the highest value used to calculate an incentive fee. A high-water mark is the highest value of the fund investment ever achieved at a performance fee crystallization date, net of fees, by the individual LP. A high-water mark clause states that a hedge fund manager must recuperate declines in value from the high-water mark before performance fees can be charged on newly generated profits. The use of high-water marks protects clients from paying twice for the same performance.

questions.los: Module 1: Alternative Investment Features, Methods, and Structures
questions.stem: In alternative investments, the American waterfall distribution method is more advantageous to the:
questions.option_a: limited partners because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis.
questions.option_b: general partner because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis.
questions.option_c: limited partners because the general partner does not participate in any profits until the hurdle rate has been met.
questions.explanation: A. Incorrect because deal-by-deal waterfalls are more advantageous to general partners (GPs), not limited partners (LPs). This allows the GP to get paid before LPs receive both their initial investment and their preferred rate of return on the entire fund. There are two types of waterfalls: deal-by-deal (or American) waterfalls and whole-of-fund (or European) waterfalls. Deal-by-deal waterfalls are more advantageous to the GP because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis, allowing the GP to get paid before LPs receive both their initial investment and their preferred rate of return (i.e., the hurdle rate) on the entire fund. B. Correct because this allows the general partner (GP) to get paid before limited partners (LPs) receive both their initial investment and their preferred rate of return on the entire fund. There are two types of waterfalls: deal-by-deal (or American) waterfalls and whole-of-fund (or European) waterfalls. Deal-by-deal waterfalls are more advantageous to the GP because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis, allowing the GP to get paid before LPs receive both their initial investment and their preferred rate of return (i.e., the hurdle rate) on the entire fund. C. Incorrect because this describes an advantage of whole-of-fund (European) waterfalls for limited partners (LPs), not deal-by-deal (American) waterfalls. There are two types of waterfalls: deal-by-deal (or American) waterfalls and whole-of-fund (or European) waterfalls. Deal-by-deal waterfalls are more advantageous to the GP because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis, allowing the GP to get paid before LPs receive both their initial investment and their preferred rate of return (i.e., the hurdle rate) on the entire fund. In whole-of-fund waterfalls, all distributions go to the LPs as deals are exited and the GP does not participate in any profits until the LPs receive their initial investment and the hurdle rate has been met. In contrast to deal-by-deal waterfalls, whole-of-fund waterfalls occur at the aggregate fund level and are more advantageous to the LPs

questions.stem: An analyst gathers the following information about a hedge fund: $200 million in assets under management at the beginning of year a 2% management fee based on year-end assets under management a 20% incentive fee calculated net of the management fee If the fund's gross return is 25% during the year, the total fees earned by the fund manager are:

questions.explanation: A. Incorrect because it is the amount if the sum of the incentive and management fees based on the dollar returns for the year ($250 million less $200 million). That is, the sum of the management fee of $1 million ($50 million times 0.02) and the incentive fee of $10 million ($50 million times 0.20), which is $11 million. That is, the total fee is the sum of the management fee of $5 million ($250 million AUM times 0.02) and the incentive fee of $9 million ($250 million less $200 million less the $5 million incentive times 0.20), which is $14 million. questions.los: Module 2: Alternative Investment Performance and Returns
questions.stem: A hedge fund has the following characteristics: Assets under management, beginning of year $100 million Assets under management, end of year $120 million Management fee 1% of year-end assets under management Performance fee 15% of the annual return above a 3% hurdle rate If the performance fee is calculated net of the management fee and there were no capital contributions or withdrawals, the net annual return to the investor is closest to:
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because the performance fee is not calculated net of the management fee: Management fee = $100 million × 120% × 1% = $1.200 million. Performance fee = [($100 million × 20%) – ($100 million × 3%)] × 15% = $2.550 million. Total fee = $1.200 million + $2.550 million = $3.750 million. Investor return = ($20 – $3.750) / $100 = 16.250% ≈ 16.3%. B.Correct because the hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return, typically 8%, that the GP must exceed in order to earn the performance fee. GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded. Management fee = $100 million × 120% × 1% = $1.200 million. Performance fee = [($100 million × 20%) – ($100 million × 3%) − $1.200 million)] × 15% = $2.370 million. Total fee = $1.200 million + $2.370 million = $3.570 million. Investor return = ($20 – $3.570) / $100 = 16.430% ≈ 16.4%. C.Incorrect because the hurdle rate is deducted from the performance fee rate rather than the rate of return: Management fee = $100 million × 120% × 1% = $1.200 million. Performance fee = [($100 million × 20%) − $1.200 million)] × (15% − 3%) = $2.256 million. Total fee = $1.200 million + $2.256 million = $3.456 million. Investor return = ($20 – $3.456) / $100 = 16.544% ≈ 16.5%

questions.los: Module 2: Alternative Investment Performance and Returns
questions.stem: An analyst collects the following information about a hedge fund: Assets under management $1.5 billion, beginning of year Annual return 20% Management fee 2%, based on year-end valuation Incentive fee 20%, calculated net of management fees If the incentive fee is calculated on returns in excess of a 6% hurdle rate, total annual fees earned by the fund manager are closest to:
questions.explanation: A.Incorrect because it fails to add the management fee to the incentive fee. The incentive fee is calculated as [$1,800,000,000 − $1,500,000,000 – ($1,500,000,000 × 6%) − $36,000,000] × 20% = $34,800,000. B.Correct because the hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return, typically 8%, that the GP must exceed in order to earn the performance fee. GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded. The management fee is calculated as $1,500,000,000 × (1 + 20%) × 2% = $36,000,000 and the incentive fee is calculated as [$1,800,000,000 − $1,500,000,000 – ($1,500,000,000 × 6%) − $36,000,000] × 20% = $34,800,000. Therefore, the total fees earned by the manager are $36,000,000 + $34,800,000 = $70,800,000. C.Incorrect because it fails to net the management fee from the incentive fee. The incentive fee is calculated as [$1,800,000,000 − $1,500,000,000 − ($1,500,000,000 × 6%)] × 20% = $42,000,000. Therefore, the total fees earned by the manager are $36,000,000 + $42,000,000 = $78,000,000.

questions.explanation: A. Incorrect because the incentive fee is not calculated independent of the management fee: Management fee = $960 million × 0.02 = $19.2 million Hard hurdle = $800 million × 0.06 = $48 million Incentive fee = ($960 million – $800 million – $48 million – $19.2 million) × 0.2 = $18.56 million Total fees = $19.2 million + $18.56 million = $37.76 million ≈ $37.8 million. B. Incorrect because the hurdle rate is calculated on the basis of ending assets under management (AUM) instead of beginning AUM: Management fee = $960 million × 0.02 = $19.2 million Hard hurdle = $960 million × 0.06 = $57.6 million Incentive fee = ($960 million – $800 million – $57.6 million) × 0.2 = $20.48 million Total fees = $19.2 million + $20.48 million = $39.68 million ≈ $39.7 million. C. Correct because the hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return, typically 8%, that the GP must exceed in order to earn the performance fee. GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded. Total fees are calculated as follows: Management fee = $960 million × 0.02 = $19.2 million Hard hurdle = $800 million × 0.06 = $48 million Incentive fee = ($960 million – $800 million – $48 million) × 0.2 = $22.4 million Total fees = $19.2 million + $22.4 million = $41.6 million.

questions.los: Module 2: Alternative Investment Performance and Returns
questions.stem: An investor gathers the following information about a hedge fund: Beginning-of-year assets under management (AUM) $300,000,000 Current high-water mark $320,000,000 Annual return before fees 10% Management fee, based on end-of-year AUM before fees 2% Incentive fee 20% If the incentive fee is based on returns net of management fees and the fee structure includes the use of a high-water mark, the investor's net return for the year is closest to:
questions.explanation: A. Incorrect because it ignores the current high-water mark and computes the incentive fee based on returns net of management fees. Accordingly, End-of-year AUM = Beginning-of-year AUM × (1 + Annual return before fees) = $300,000,000 × (1 + 10%) = $330,000,000. Management fee = Management fee based on end-of-year AUM × End-of-year AUM = 2% × $330,000,000 = $6,600,000. Return net of management fee = End-of-year AUM – Beginning-of-year AUM – Management fee = $330,000,000 – $300,000,000 – $6,600,000 = $23,400,000. Incentive fee = 20% × Return net of management fee = 20% × $23,400,000 = $4,680,000. Total fees = Management fee + Incentive fee = $6,600,000 + $4,680,000 = $11,280,000. Net return = (End-of-year AUM – Beginning-of-year AUM – Total fees) / Beginning-of-year AUM = ($330,000,000 – $300,000,000 – $11,280,000) / $300,000,000 = $18,720,000 / $300,000,000 = 6.24%. B. Incorrect because the current high-water mark is used as a cap for management fee and incentive fee (instead of the threshold representing the highest cumulative return above which an incentive fee is calculated). Accordingly, Management fee = Management fee based on end-of-year AUM × Current high-water mark = 2% × $320,000,000 = $6,400,000. Return net of management fee and capped by current high-water mark = Current high-water mark – Beginning-of-year AUM – Management fee = $320,000,000 – $300,000,000 – $6,400,000 = $13,600,000. Incentive fee = 20% × Return net of management fee = 20% × $13,600,000 = $2,720,000. Total fees = Management fee + Incentive fee = $6,400,000 + $2,720,000 = $9,120,000. Net return = (End-of-year AUM – Beginning-of-year AUM – Total fees) / Beginning-of-year AUM = ($330,000,000 – $300,000,000 – $9,120,000) / $300,000,000 = $20,880,000 / $300,000,000 = 6.96%. C. Correct because in hedge funds, fee calculations also take into account a high-water mark, which reﬂects the highest value used to calculate an incentive fee. A high-water mark is the highest value of the fund investment ever achieved at a performance fee crystallization date, net of fees, by the individual LP. A high-water mark clause states that a hedge fund manager must recuperate declines in value from the high-water mark before performance fees can be charged on newly generated profits. End-of-year AUM = Beginning-of-year AUM × (1 + Annual return before fees) = $300,000,000 × (1 + 10%) = $330,000,000. Management fee = Management fee based on end-of-year AUM × End-of-year AUM = 2% × $330,000,000 = $6,600,000. The incentive fee is payable if the current high water-mark is exceeded and is based on the excess return above this high-water mark. Return in excess of current high-water mark = End-of-year AUM – Current high-water mark – Management fee = $330,000,000 – $320,000,000 – $6,600,000 = $3,400,000. Incentive fee = 20% × Return in excess of current high-water mark = 20% × $3,400,000 = $680,000. Total fees = Management fee + Incentive fee (as applicable) = $6,600,000 + $680,000 = $7,280,000. Net return = (End-of-year AUM – Beginning-of-year AUM – Total fees) / Beginning-of-year AUM = ($330,000,000 – $300,000,000 – $7,280,000) / $300,000,000 = $22,720,000 / $300,000,000 ≈ 7.57%.

questions.los: Module 2: Alternative Investment Performance and Returns
questions.stem: A hedge fund has the following characteristics: Initial investment capital of $200 million; 2% management fee, based on assets under management at the end of the year; 20% incentive fee, calculated independent of the management fee and based on returns in excess of a 7% hurdle rate. If the fund's return is 18% at the end of the first year, the fund's investors' net return is closest to:

B. Correct because the partnership agreement usually specifies that the performance fee is earned only after the fund achieves a return known as a hurdle rate. The hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return, typically 8%, that the GP must exceed in order to earn the performance fee. GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded. Accordingly, (in $ millions): AUM at the beginning of the year: 200 AUM at the end of the year: 200 × (1 + 0.18) = 236 Management fee: 236 × 0.02 = 4.72 Incentive fee: [236 – 200 – (200 × 0.07)] × 0.20 = 4.40 Total fees paid to the hedge fund manager: 4.72 + 4.40 = 9.12 Investor's return: (236 – 200 – 9.12) ÷ 200 = 13.44% ≈ 13.4%. C. Incorrect because the incentive fee is calculated net of the management fee (in $ millions): Management fee: 236 × 0.02 = 4.72 Incentive fee: [236 – 200 – (200 × 0.07) – 4.72] × 0.20 = 3.456 Investor's return: (236 – 200 – 4.72 – 3.456) ÷ 200 = 13.912% ≈ 13.9%.
